newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia urged to still resist devaluation call.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia urged to still resist devaluation call.

text.p: Independent Yugoslav economists said on Monday there was no need to devalue the dinar whose stability in 1996, despite an expanding trade gap and soaring inflation, has surprised some analysts.
"The exchange rate of the dinar is realistic and balanced," Zoran Popov of the Economic Institute told Reuters.
He said internal pressure for devaluation, which the government is resisting, stemmed mainly from the inefficient state sector of industry.
"In a country with parallel official and grey economies, it is the official sector which wants devaluation to increase its competitiveness abroad," Popov said.
After suffering inflation up to 60 percent a day in 1993, Yugoslavia introduced a new dinar, pegging it at par to the German mark.
It was devalued by 70 percent to 3.3 to the mark last November.
Danijel Cvijeticanin of the Economic Institute said dinar stability was a paradox.
"An expanding trade gap normally reflects on the exchange rate and prices. In Yugoslavia we have a stable exchange rate despite soaring prices," he said.
Cvijeticanin said the paradox could result from several factors.
"The state has administratively protected the dinar rate but not prices and the central bank intervened on the interbank forex market from its reserves to keep the rate stable," he said.
When last devaluing the dinar, monetary authorities may have still left it overvalued and with enough room to compensate for 1996 inflation, he said.
Cvijeticanin questioned the level of the trade gap as reported by official statistics, saying it may not be as large as $1.7 billion.
Other economists agreed devaluation was not a remedy and said it would only lead to higher inflation.

"Inflation is present only in the official economy and this segment calls for devaluation to make up for its inefficiency," Zoran Popov said, citing low capacity utilisation and huge costs as key reasons for inefficiency.

Popov praised the government's resistance to devaluation calls and said the biggest achievement of the 1996 economic policy was not to allow creation of two parallel foreign exchange markets -- one for the state and public companies and another for the household and private sector.

"It is good the state did not give in to pressures from big companies to devalue. Our state companies can spend all they are given," he said, adding that the hard currency needs of the official sector were large, but effective demand was low due to the sector's insolvency.
Economists said one side would have to give in but hopefully not the state.
"Companies must reduce their prices and the state must lower their fiscal burden, reduce public spending and start restructuring," Popov said.
Popov said high costs of the official economy resulted from enormous companies' fiscal burden, which serves to finance huge public spending.

"To discontinue the vicious circle, the state needs to embark on privatisation and restructuring to increase competitiveness. It will also have to reduce public spending, but those are long-term processes."
Miroljub Labus, another economist with the institute, said the dinar rate was not the key issue of Yugoslav economic pains. "We should pay more attention to structural problems instead," he said.
($1 = 4.9421 dinars) -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
